blocks.AB_ON_START_TOOLTIP: Runs once when the game starts.
blocks.AB_ON_UPDATE_TOOLTIP: Runs on every frame, 30 times per second.
blocks.AB_ON_EVERY_TOOLTIP: Runs again and again with this many milliseconds between.
blocks.AB_ON_DRAW_TOOLTIP: Draw your own graphics here. Runs after the sprites are drawn.
blocks.AB_SPLASH_TOOLTIP: Shows a message and waits until A is pressed.
blocks.AB_SPLASH_SCREEN_TOOLTIP: Clears the screen, runs the drawing blocks inside, shows the result and waits until A is pressed.
blocks.AB_GAME_OVER_TOOLTIP: Ends the game and shows the score.
blocks.AB_PAUSE_TOOLTIP: Waits for a number of milliseconds.
blocks.AB_PARTICLE_PIXEL: emit 1 px particle at x %1 y %2 start velocity x %3 y %4 lifetime %5 ms end velocity x %6 y %7 color %8
blocks.AB_PARTICLE_IMAGE: emit image particle %1 at x %2 y %3 start velocity x %4 y %5 lifetime %6 ms end velocity x %7 y %8 color %9
blocks.AB_PARTICLE_PIXEL_TOOLTIP: Velocity changes linearly from start to end over the lifetime, in pixels per second. World coordinates. Up to 12 particles on Nano or 16 on Arduboy, no collisions. Place inside a sprite overlap event to trigger on contact.
blocks.AB_PARTICLE_IMAGE_TOOLTIP: Velocity changes linearly from start to end over the lifetime, in pixels per second. World coordinates. Up to 12 particles on Nano or 16 on Arduboy, no collisions. Place inside a sprite overlap event to trigger on contact.
blocks.AB_EFFECT_TOOLTIP: A particle effect recipe. Put part blocks inside to choose how the particles look and move, then send them out with the emit block. Parts you leave out keep their default.
blocks.AB_FX_IMAGE_TOOLTIP: Each particle is an image. An image with several frames plays them over the lifetime, for example smoke that grows.
blocks.AB_FX_LIFE_TOOLTIP: Each particle lives a random time between the two values, in milliseconds.
blocks.AB_FX_DIRECTION_TOOLTIP: Which way the particles fly, in degrees: 0 up, 90 right, 180 down, -90 left. Spread adds a random angle; 180 sends them in all directions.
blocks.AB_FX_SPEED_TOOLTIP: Start speed in pixels per second, random between the two values.
blocks.AB_FX_AREA_TOOLTIP: The particles start at random places in a rectangle this wide and high, centred where they are sent out. Use a wide area for rain.
blocks.AB_FX_ACCEL_TOOLTIP: A steady push in pixels per second per second. Positive y pulls down like gravity; negative y makes smoke rise.
blocks.AB_FX_DRAG_TOOLTIP: How much of the speed is lost each second. Makes explosions and smoke slow down.
blocks.AB_FX_WOBBLE_TOOLTIP: A random sideways nudge every frame, for smoke and flames.
blocks.AB_FX_BLINK_TOOLTIP: The particles blink during the last part of their lifetime, so they fade out on the black and white screen.
blocks.AB_FX_BURST_TOOLTIP: Sends out particles from an effect at a place in the world. Rotated turns the effect's direction, for example to spray where the player is facing. Up to 12 particles on Nano or 16 on Arduboy at a time.
blocks.AB_FX_BURST_FROM_TOOLTIP: Sends out particles from an effect at the middle of a sprite. Put it in an 'every' event for a smoke trail.
blocks.AB_FX_CLEAR_TOOLTIP: Removes the particles of one effect.
blocks.AB_INVERT_TOOLTIP: Swaps black and white on the screen.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_CREATE_TOOLTIP: Creates a new sprite in the middle of the screen.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_PROJECTILE_TOOLTIP: Creates a moving sprite that disappears when it leaves the screen.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_PROP_TOOLTIP: Sets a value of a sprite.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_CHANGE_PROP_TOOLTIP: Changes a value of a sprite.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_POSITION_TOOLTIP: Moves the sprite. x and y are the middle of the sprite.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_OUTLINE_WIDTH_TOOLTIP: Thickness from 1 to 8 pixels. Default is 1. Choose an outline color with the outline block.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_Z_TOOLTIP: Sprites on a higher layer are drawn on top. Default is 0, from -128 to 127.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_OUTLINE_TOOLTIP: Outline around the sprite shape. Automatic uses white on black backgrounds and black on white.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_IMAGE_TOOLTIP: Changes the picture of the sprite.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_STAY_IN_SCREEN_TOOLTIP: Prevents the sprite from leaving the screen.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_FLAG_TOOLTIP: Turns a behaviour of the sprite on or off.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_ANIMATE_TOOLTIP: Shows the frames of the image one after another. 0 stops.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_DESTROY_ALL_TOOLTIP: Removes all sprites of a kind.
blocks.AB_ON_OVERLAP: on %1 of kind %2 overlaps %3 of kind %4
blocks.AB_SPRITE_OVERLAPS_TOOLTIP: True if the two sprites touch.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_IS_HITTING_TOOLTIP: True if the sprite hit a wall or the screen edge on that side in this frame.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_IS_KIND_TOOLTIP: True if the sprite is of this kind.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_SET_KIND_TOOLTIP: Changes the kind of the sprite.
blocks.AB_SPRITE_EXISTS_TOOLTIP: True if the sprite has not been destroyed.
blocks.AB_FOR_EACH_KIND_TOOLTIP: Runs the blocks inside once for every sprite of the kind.
blocks.AB_ON_BUTTON_TOOLTIP: Runs when a button is pressed or released.
blocks.AB_IS_PRESSED_TOOLTIP: True while the button is held down.
blocks.AB_MOVE_SPRITE_TOOLTIP: The direction buttons move the sprite. Use 0 to lock a direction.
blocks.AB_SET_TILEMAP_TOOLTIP: Shows a tile map. Solid tiles work as walls.
blocks.AB_CAMERA_FOLLOW_TOOLTIP: Moves the view so the sprite stays in the middle.
blocks.AB_SET_CAMERA_TOOLTIP: Moves the view. x and y are the top left corner.
blocks.AB_CAMERA_X_TOOLTIP: Left edge of the view in the world.
blocks.AB_CAMERA_Y_TOOLTIP: Top edge of the view in the world.
blocks.AB_SHAKE_TOOLTIP: Shakes the camera. Strength is how many pixels it moves (at most 16), ms is how long it lasts.
blocks.AB_BG_SET_TOOLTIP: Draws a background behind everything else. Use it again to switch to another background. Make backgrounds in the Backgrounds tab.
blocks.AB_BG_CLEAR_TOOLTIP: Removes the background, so the screen behind everything is black.
blocks.AB_BG_SET_POSITION_TOOLTIP: Moves the background on the screen. It repeats, so the screen is always filled.
blocks.AB_BG_CHANGE_POSITION_TOOLTIP: Moves the background a little. Put it in "on game update" for a background that keeps scrolling.
blocks.AB_BG_X_TOOLTIP: Where the background is drawn, left and right.
blocks.AB_BG_Y_TOOLTIP: Where the background is drawn, up and down.
blocks.AB_SPAWN_ON_TILES: on every %1 tile place sprite %2 of kind %3
blocks.AB_SPAWN_ON_TILES_TOOLTIP: Creates a sprite on each tile of this type and removes the tile.
blocks.AB_ON_TILE: on %1 of kind %2 overlaps tile %3 at %4 %5
blocks.AB_ON_TILE_TOOLTIP: Runs when a sprite touches a tile. The column and row of the tile are in the variables.
blocks.AB_SET_TILE: set tile at col %1 row %2 to %3
blocks.AB_SET_TILE_TOOLTIP: Changes one tile of the map.
blocks.AB_TILE_IS_TOOLTIP: True if the tile is of this type.
blocks.AB_PLACE_ON_TILE_TOOLTIP: Moves the sprite to the middle of a tile.
blocks.AB_SCORE_SET_TOOLTIP: Sets the score. It is shown in the top right corner.
blocks.AB_SCORE_POSITION_TOOLTIP: Moves the score display to screen coordinates x and y.
blocks.AB_LIFE_SET_TOOLTIP: Sets the number of lives. They are shown as hearts.
blocks.AB_LIFE_CHANGE_TOOLTIP: Adds to the lives. At 0 the game is over.
blocks.AB_ON_LIFE_ZERO_TOOLTIP: Runs when the lives reach 0, instead of game over.
blocks.AB_HISCORE_TOOLTIP: The best score, saved on the device.
blocks.AB_STORAGE_SAVE_TOOLTIP: Saves a number that is kept when the device is turned off. Slots 0 to 31.
blocks.AB_DRAW_PIXEL_TOOLTIP: Draws one pixel. Use inside "on draw".
blocks.AB_DRAW_LINE: draw line from x %1 y %2 to x %3 y %4 %5
blocks.AB_DRAW_LINE_TOOLTIP: Draws a line. Use inside "on draw".
blocks.AB_DRAW_RECT: draw %1 rectangle x %2 y %3 w %4 h %5 %6
blocks.AB_DRAW_RECT_TOOLTIP: Draws a rectangle. Use inside "on draw".
blocks.AB_DRAW_CIRCLE_TOOLTIP: Draws a circle. Use inside "on draw".
blocks.AB_DRAW_IMAGE_TOOLTIP: Draws an image with its top left corner at x and y.
blocks.AB_GET_PIXEL: pixel at x %1 y %2 is on
blocks.AB_GET_PIXEL_TOOLTIP: True if the pixel is white.
blocks.AB_PLAY_TONE_TOOLTIP: Plays a tone. 440 Hz is the note A.
blocks.AB_PLAY_SONG_TOOLTIP: Plays a ready made song in the background, with melody, harmony, bass and drums.
blocks.AB_STOP_SONG_TOOLTIP: Stops the song. Sound effects and melodies go on.
blocks.AB_PITCH_TOOLTIP: Each sound inside gets a random pitch between the two numbers. 100 is the normal pitch, 90 is a little lower and 110 a little higher. Good for jump sounds that are a little different every time.
blocks.AB_PLAY_MELODY_TOOLTIP: Plays music in the background. Notes C D E F G A B, R is a rest. Add a number for the octave (C5) and :beats for the length (G:2, E:1/2).
blocks.AB_NOTE_TOOLTIP: The frequency of a note, for the tone block.
blocks.AB_RANDOM_TOOLTIP: A random whole number between the two numbers.
blocks.AB_MINMAX_TOOLTIP: The smaller or the bigger of two numbers.
blocks.AB_CPP_TOOLTIP: C++ code that is copied into the game. It runs on the device, but not in the simulator.
blocks.AB_MAP_TOOLTIP: Scale a value between ranges. Integer result; values outside the range are extrapolated. If the source limits are equal, returns the target lower limit.
blocks.AB_TIMER_SET_TOOLTIP: Sets the time in seconds. 94 seconds displays as 01:34 in mm:ss format. Supports Math and Random. Range: 0–32767 seconds.
blocks.AB_TIMER_CHANGE_TOOLTIP: Adds time; use a negative number to subtract. Time stays between 0 and 32767 seconds.
blocks.AB_TIMER_RUN_TOOLTIP: Counts once per second, or stops. Countdown stops at zero. Each timer runs independently.
blocks.AB_TIMER_FORMAT_TOOLTIP: Chooses the display format. Minutes and hours alone show whole elapsed units. Hiding does not stop the timer.
blocks.AB_TIMER_POSITION_TOOLTIP: Moves this timer display to screen coordinates x and y.
blocks.AB_TIMER_VALUE_TOOLTIP: Total seconds in this timer. Use with Math, Random or conditions; also fits the sprite position block.
blocks.AB_TIMER_SET_MILLIS_TOOLTIP: Sets the fractional second (0–999). Set seconds to 94 and this to 125 for 01:34.125.
blocks.AB_TIMER_CHANGE_MILLIS_TOOLTIP: Adds milliseconds, carrying into seconds. Negative values subtract.
blocks.AB_TIMER_MILLIS_TOOLTIP: The millisecond part (0–999), alongside the seconds block. Not total milliseconds.
blocks.AB_INFO_POSITION_TOOLTIP: Moves score, health or a created timer. Choose New timer to create another independent timer.

ui.docs.title: Documentation
ui.docs.start.title: Getting started
ui.docs.start.body:
ArduCade lets you make your own games for Arduboy and other small game devices. The screen is 128 dots wide and 64 dots tall, and each dot is either lit or dark. You make the game by putting blocks together, and you can try it right away in the simulator.

Press “New” to start. You can begin with an empty project or pick a game template. To learn step by step, press “Guides” and play through the levels.

Projects are saved in the browser automatically, and you find them again under “My projects”. “Save” stores the game as a file you can share or open again later. The file is an image that looks like a game cartridge, and the whole game is stored inside the picture. Open it again with “Open file”. Do not edit the image in a photo app, or the game may be lost.
ui.docs.blocks.title: Blocks and events
ui.docs.blocks.body:
The blocks are sorted into categories on the left of the editor. Drag a block into the workspace and snap it onto another block. Press the (i) on a block to read about it here. You can also right click or press and hold a block and choose “About this block”.

A game is made of events. “on start” runs once when the game starts. “on game update” runs many times a second, and button events run when a button is pressed. Blocks that are not attached to an event do not run.

Round blocks give a number, a text or a sprite, and go into the holes of other blocks. Hexagonal blocks are true or false, and are used in “if” blocks and loops.
ui.docs.assets.title: Sprites, tiles and tile maps
ui.docs.assets.body:
In the “Sprites” tab you draw the characters of the game, dot by dot. A sprite can have several frames that make an animation. Each sprite has a kind, such as player, enemy or coin. The kind is used to find out what hit what.

In the “Tiles” tab you draw small squares such as ground, walls and water. You can make a tile solid, so sprites cannot pass through it.

In the “Tile map” tab you put tiles together into a level. The level can be bigger than the screen, and the camera can follow the player.
ui.docs.sim.title: The simulator
ui.docs.sim.body:
The simulator on the right runs the game while you build it. Press Play to start and stop to end. The game restarts when you change the blocks.

You play with the buttons below the screen, also by touch on tablets. On a keyboard, use the arrow keys or WASD to move, Z or Space for A and X or Enter for B.

You can show the simulator on its own in a large size, and turn the sound on and off.
ui.docs.sound.title: Sound and music
ui.docs.sound.body:
ArduCade has three kinds of sound. You find them all in the Music category.

Sound effects are short sounds for things that happen in the game, like a jump, a coin or an explosion. Use “play sound”.

Melodies are tunes you write yourself with note letters, one note at a time. Use “play melody”.

Songs are ready made music with four voices at once: melody, harmony, bass and drums. Use “play song” for music on the title screen, in a level or in a boss fight, and for short tunes when a level is done, when the game is lost and when it is won.

Sound effects play on top of melodies and songs. “stop song” stops only the song, and “stop sound” stops everything. Melodies and songs also stop when the game is over.

The simulator plays songs like an Arduboy does. Consoles without an ATmega32u4, like the Nano consoles, the ESPboy and the ATtiny85 console, play songs with one voice and no drums.

The songs are played by ATMlib (Arduboy Tracker Music) by TEAM a.r.g., Davey Taylor and Joeri Gantois, under the BSD 3-Clause License. The license is in the file ab_atm.h, which comes with every exported Arduino sketch.
ui.docs.shortcuts.title: Keyboard shortcuts
ui.docs.shortcuts.body:
Everything in ArduCade works with the mouse and with touch on a tablet. With a keyboard you can work faster: the shortcuts below save, start the game and switch between tabs without reaching for the mouse.

On a Mac, use ⌘ (Command) and ⌥ (Option). On Windows and Linux, use Ctrl and Alt. Press ? in the editor to open this page.

The editor shortcuts work everywhere in the editor, except / and ?, which do nothing while you type in a text field or a code editor. The simulator keys work when you are not typing in a field, so you can test the game right after changing a block.

ui.docs.device.title: Play on a real device
ui.docs.device.body:
When the game is ready, you can play it on an Arduboy or a home made device. In the “Device” panel you choose which device you have. Press “Compile” to turn the game into code the device understands. You then see how much space the game uses.

Connect the device with USB and press “Upload to device”. This works in Chrome and Edge. For devices that cannot be compiled in the browser, download the sketch and use the Arduino IDE.

Want to see the code behind the blocks? The C++, JavaScript and Python tabs show the game as text.

Built something even smaller? Some settings only show up for those who are patient with the settings button.
ui.docs.ex.ab_on_start: When the game starts, a sprite is made and placed in the middle of the screen.
ui.docs.ex.ab_on_update: While A is held down, the sprite moves one dot to the right every time the game updates.
ui.docs.ex.ab_on_every: The player gets one point every second (1000 milliseconds).
ui.docs.ex.ab_move_sprite: The sprite can be steered with the arrow buttons. The numbers are how fast it moves sideways and up and down.
ui.docs.ex.ab_on_button: When A is pressed, a projectile is shot straight up from the sprite. A minus speed means upwards.
ui.docs.ex.ab_on_overlap: When the player touches a coin, the player gets one point and the coin disappears.
ui.docs.ex.ab_sprite_stay_in_screen: The sprite is created and then cannot leave the screen.
ui.docs.ex.ab_sprite_set_flag: The sprite cannot leave the screen.
ui.docs.ex.ab_on_life_zero: When the player has lost all lives, the game is lost.
ui.docs.ex.ab_draw_text: Shows the score in the top left corner. “create text with” makes one text from “Score: ” and the number.
ui.docs.ex.ab_play_melody: A number after a colon is the length in beats. The length also applies to the notes after it, until you write a new one. Here E and F are two beats, G, A and B half a beat, and the high C (C5) four beats.
ui.docs.ex.ab_play_song: The title theme starts with the game and repeats. When the last life is lost, the game over tune plays once. The pause lets it finish before the game is over.
ui.docs.ex.ab_pitch: The jump sound gets a slightly different pitch each time, so it does not get boring.
ui.docs.ex.ab_random: Every second the sprite moves to a random place at the top of the screen.
ui.docs.ex.controls_if: If the score gets above 9, the player has won.
ui.docs.ex.procedures_defnoreturn: A function gathers blocks under one name. Here “restart” resets score and lives, and is used when the game starts.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_start:
Runs once, when the game starts and again each time it restarts after game over. Put everything the game needs at the beginning here: make the player sprite, choose the tile map, set the score and lives.

Only blocks attached inside an event block run. A loose block lying in the workspace does nothing.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_update:
Runs again and again while the game is going, 30 times every second. Use it for things that must be checked all the time, like whether a button is held down or whether the score is high enough to win.

The sprites move on their own from their speed, so you do not need to move them here.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_every:
Runs again and again with a pause between, measured in milliseconds. 1000 milliseconds is one second, so 500 means twice a second.

Good for things that happen at a steady pace: new enemies arriving, a clock counting down, or a point every second.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_draw:
Draw your own text, lines and shapes here. It runs on every frame, after the tile map and the sprites are drawn, so what you draw ends up on top.

The screen is cleared before each frame, so the drawing must be done again every time. That is why the drawing blocks belong inside this event.
ui.docs.more.ab_splash:
Shows a message in a box in the middle of the screen. The game stops and waits until the player presses A, then it continues.

Use it for short messages like “Level 2!” or the rules of the game. Only the first 31 letters are shown.
ui.docs.more.ab_splash_screen:
Makes your own start screen or picture. The screen is cleared, the drawing blocks inside are drawn, and the game waits until the player presses A.

Put text and images inside to make a title screen, or a picture between levels.
ui.docs.more.ab_game_over:
Ends the game. The screen shows GAME OVER or YOU WIN!, the score and the best score, and a sound plays. When the player presses A, the game starts again from “on start”.

Choose lose or win in the list.
ui.docs.more.ab_pause:
Stops the whole game for a number of milliseconds. Nothing moves while it waits. 1000 milliseconds is one second.

Use short pauses, for example a little stop after the player is hit.
ui.docs.more.ab_runtime:
How many milliseconds have gone by since the game started. 1000 milliseconds is one second.

You can use it to make a timer, or to check how long something has taken.
ui.docs.more.ab_invert: Swaps black and white on the whole screen. Turn it on and off to make the screen flash, for example when the player is hit or wins.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_create:
Makes a new sprite with this image and kind, in the middle of the screen. A sprite is a figure that can move, bump into things and be animated.

Put it in a variable (set mySprite to ...) so you can use the sprite later with the other sprite blocks. The kind is used to find out what touched what, for example Player, Enemy or Food.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_projectile:
Makes a sprite that starts at another sprite and flies away with this speed. It is removed by itself when it leaves the screen or hits a wall.

vx is the speed sideways and vy up and down, in pixels per second. A minus number in vy means upwards. Good for bullets, arrows and fireballs.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_prop:
Sets one value of a sprite to a number. Choose the value in the list:

x and y is the position of the middle of the sprite. vx and vy is the speed in pixels per second. ax and ay is the acceleration: how much the speed changes every second, for example gravity. left, right, top and bottom move the sprite so that edge is at the number.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_change_prop:
Adds a number to one value of a sprite. A minus number makes the value smaller. “change x by 1” moves the sprite one pixel to the right.

The values are the same as in the set block: position, speed, acceleration and the edges of the sprite.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_get_prop:
Gives one value of a sprite as a number: position, speed, acceleration, width, height or one of the edges.

For example, check if the bottom of the player is below 60 to find out if it has fallen off the screen.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_position:
Moves the sprite straight to a place. x is from left to right and y from top to bottom. The screen is 128 pixels wide and 64 pixels tall, so x 64 y 32 is the middle.

The position is the middle of the sprite.

You can also insert a timer value block in place of the sprite to move that timer’s display. For a timer, x and y are the top-left corner in screen pixels, independent of the camera.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_velocity:
Gives the sprite a speed, in pixels per second. The sprite then keeps moving on its own until you change the speed.

vx is sideways: plus to the right and minus to the left. vy is up and down: plus downwards and minus upwards. 0 and 0 makes the sprite stand still.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_stay_in_screen: Keeps the sprite within the screen. The sprite stops at the edge, including when it moves with buttons, velocity, or gravity. Put this block in “on start” after creating the sprite.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_flag:
Turns a behaviour of the sprite on or off:

Stay in screen: cannot leave the screen. Stay in map: cannot leave the tile map. Bounce on wall: turns around when it hits a wall or the edge. Ghost: goes through walls and does not touch other sprites. Auto destroy: is removed when it leaves the screen. Destroy on wall: is removed when it hits a wall. Invisible: is not drawn, but still takes part in the game.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_animate:
Shows the frames of the sprite image one after another, like a flip book. The number is how many milliseconds each frame is shown. 0 stops the animation.

You draw the frames in the Sprites tab.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_image: Changes the picture of the sprite. For example, show a picture facing left when the player walks left, and one facing right when it walks right.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_outline: Draws an outline around the shape of the sprite, so it can be seen on any background. Automatic picks white on dark backgrounds and black on light ones. Off removes the outline.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_outline_width: How thick the outline around the sprite is, from 1 to 8 pixels. Choose the outline color with the outline block first.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_z: Chooses which sprites are drawn on top when they overlap. Sprites on a higher layer are drawn over sprites on a lower layer. All sprites start on layer 0.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_destroy: Removes the sprite from the game. It is no longer drawn and cannot touch anything. Use it for a coin that is picked up or an enemy that is beaten.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_destroy_all: Removes all sprites of one kind at once, for example all enemies when a new level starts.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_overlap:
Runs when a sprite of one kind touches a sprite of another kind. Inside the block, the variables sprite and otherSprite are the two sprites that touch, so you can do something with exactly those.

The event runs on every frame as long as they touch. To make it happen only once, destroy one of them or move it away.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_overlaps: True if the two sprites touch each other right now, otherwise false. Use it in an “if” block.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_is_hitting:
True if the sprite bumped into a wall or the edge of the screen on that side in this frame.

In a platform game, “is hitting wall bottom” tells you that the player is standing on the ground and is allowed to jump.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_is_kind: True if the sprite is of this kind. Useful in “for each” loops and events where you need to know what kind of sprite you have.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_set_kind: Changes the kind of a sprite. For example, an enemy can turn into Food when it is beaten, so the player can pick it up.
ui.docs.more.ab_sprite_exists: True if the sprite is still in the game, false if it has been destroyed. Check this before you use a sprite that may have been removed.
ui.docs.more.ab_for_each_kind:
Runs the blocks inside once for every sprite of this kind. The variable is the sprite the loop is at right now.

For example, make all enemies move towards the player, or give all coins a new speed.
ui.docs.more.ab_move_sprite:
Lets the player steer the sprite with the arrow buttons. vx is the speed sideways and vy the speed up and down, in pixels per second.

Use 0 to lock a direction. In a platform game you often only want to steer sideways, so vy is 0.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_button:
Runs once each time a button is pressed, or released. Choose the button and pressed or released in the lists.

Good for things that should happen once per press, like a jump or a shot. To do something as long as a button is held down, use “is button pressed” in “on game update” instead.

The list also offers any button, any direction button, and A+B. A+B runs when A is pressed or released while B is held, or B is pressed or released while A is held.
ui.docs.more.ab_is_pressed: True as long as the button is held down. Use it in an “if” block inside “on game update” to make something happen all the time while the player holds the button.
ui.docs.more.ab_set_tilemap:
Shows a tile map made in the Tile map tab. Each tile is 8 by 8 pixels. Tiles you have made solid work as walls and floors that sprites cannot pass through.

The map can be bigger than the screen. Use “camera follow” to see the rest of it.
ui.docs.more.ab_camera_follow:
Moves the view so the sprite stays in the middle of the screen. The camera stops at the edges of the tile map so you do not see outside it.

Use it when the map is bigger than the screen.
ui.docs.more.ab_set_camera: Moves the view to a place in the world. x and y are the top left corner of what you see. This stops “camera follow”.
ui.docs.more.ab_camera_x: Where the left edge of the view is in the world. Useful to draw things that move with the camera, or to place sprites just outside what the player sees.
ui.docs.more.ab_camera_y: Where the top edge of the view is in the world.
ui.docs.more.ab_spawn_on_tiles:
Finds every tile of this type in the tile map, puts a new sprite there and removes the tile.

This lets you place coins and enemies directly in the map editor, by drawing a special tile where they should be. Put it in “on start” after the tile map is set.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_tile:
Runs when a sprite of this kind touches a tile of this type. The variables col and row tell which tile it is, so you can change or remove exactly that tile.

Good for spikes, doors, flags and things to pick up in the map. The event runs on every frame as long as they touch.
ui.docs.more.ab_set_tile:
Changes one tile in the map. col is the column counted from the left and row the row counted from the top, both starting at 0.

Use it to open a door, remove a picked up item or build bridges while the game is running.
ui.docs.more.ab_tile_is: True if the tile at that column and row is of this type. Use it to check what is next to the player, for example if there is water ahead.
ui.docs.more.ab_place_on_tile: Moves the sprite to the middle of a tile in the map. Easier than counting pixels: column 3 row 2 is the fourth tile from the left and the third from the top.
ui.docs.more.ab_score_set: Sets the score to a number. The score is shown in the top right corner of the screen as soon as you use a score block. Set it to 0 in “on start”.
ui.docs.more.ab_score_change: Adds to the score. Use 1 to get one point, or a minus number to lose points.
ui.docs.more.ab_score: The score right now, as a number. Use it to check if the player has won, or show it with “draw text”.
ui.docs.more.ab_life_set: Sets the number of lives. The lives are shown as hearts in the top left corner.
ui.docs.more.ab_life_change: Adds to the number of lives. Use -1 when the player is hurt. When the lives reach 0, the game is over, unless you use “on life zero”.
ui.docs.more.ab_life: The number of lives right now.
ui.docs.more.ab_on_life_zero: Runs when the lives reach 0. Without this block the game ends with game over. With it, you decide what happens: for example show a message and start the level again.
ui.docs.more.ab_hiscore: The best score ever reached on this device. It is saved by itself at game over and is kept when the device is turned off.
ui.docs.more.ab_storage_save: Saves a number in one of 32 slots (0 to 31). The number is kept when the device is turned off, so you can remember things like the last level or the settings.
ui.docs.more.ab_storage_load: Reads the number saved in a slot. A slot where nothing has been saved yet gives 0.
ui.docs.more.ab_particle_pixel:
Makes a small dot that flies off and disappears by itself after the lifetime in milliseconds. The speed changes smoothly from the start speed to the end speed.

Use many of them for sparks, dust or explosions, for example in an overlap event. Particles do not bump into anything, and there can only be a few at a time.
ui.docs.more.ab_particle_image: Like the pixel particle, but with an image. Good for small stars, smoke or pieces that fly off when something breaks.
ui.docs.more.ab_particles_clear: Removes all particles from the screen at once.
ui.diag.noEffect: There is no effect called {name}. Make one with the effect block.
ui.diag.duplicateEffect: Two effects are called {name}. Give them different names.
ui.docs.more.ab_effect:
An effect is a recipe for particles. Stack part blocks inside: how they look, how long they live, which way and how fast they fly, and forces such as gravity, drag and wobble. Parts you leave out keep their default, and if a part is there twice the last one counts.

The recipe does nothing on its own. Use emit to send particles out, as often as you like. Start from one of the ready made effects and change the numbers.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_burst:
Sends out a number of particles from an effect at x and y in the world.

Rotated turns the whole effect: a spray that points right (90°) points left when rotated 180. Put it in an 'every' event to keep an effect going, such as rain or smoke.
ui.docs.more.ab_draw_text:
Writes text on the screen. x and y are the top left corner of the text. Each letter is 6 pixels wide, so about 21 letters fit on a line.

Put it inside “on draw”, otherwise the text is cleared away straight away. Use “create text with” to put text and numbers together.
ui.docs.more.text: A piece of text. Write anything between the quotes and use it in blocks that show text.
ui.docs.more.text_join: Puts several pieces of text and numbers together into one text, for example “Score: ” and the score. Press the gear to add more pieces.
ui.docs.more.ab_draw_pixel: Draws one dot on the screen. x is from 0 to 127 and y from 0 to 63. Use inside “on draw”.
ui.docs.more.ab_draw_line: Draws a straight line from one point to another. Use inside “on draw”.
ui.docs.more.ab_draw_rect: Draws a rectangle. x and y are the top left corner, w is the width and h the height. Choose outline or filled. Use inside “on draw”.
ui.docs.more.ab_draw_circle: Draws a circle. x and y are the center and r is the radius, the distance from the center to the edge. Choose outline or filled. Use inside “on draw”.
ui.docs.more.ab_draw_image: Draws an image from the Sprites tab, with its top left corner at x and y. It is only a picture: it does not move or touch anything like a sprite. Use inside “on draw” or in a splash screen.
ui.docs.more.ab_get_pixel: True if the dot at x and y is lit (white) right now. Use it inside “on draw” to check what has been drawn.
ui.docs.more.ab_play_effect:
Plays a short ready made sound. The game keeps going while the sound plays.

The list is sorted by use: moving (jump, step, land, dash, bounce), collecting (coin, gem, key, power up, extra life, heal), fighting (shoot, laser, hit, hurt, enemy defeated, shield, falling bomb, explosion), menus (blip, select, back, error) and events (door, teleport, alarm, win, lose).

Only the sounds the game plays take up space on the device.
ui.docs.more.ab_play_melody:
Plays music in the background while the game keeps going. Write notes with the letters C D E F G A B (H also works). R is a rest.

A number after the letter is the octave: C5 is higher than C4. A number after a colon is the length in beats: G:2 is two beats, E:1/2 half a beat. The octave and the length carry on to the next notes until you write a new one.

The tempo is beats per minute: a higher number plays faster. Choose once or repeat.
ui.docs.more.ab_play_tone: Plays one tone with a frequency in hertz for a number of milliseconds. A higher number gives a brighter tone. Use the note block if you would rather choose a note by name.
ui.docs.more.ab_note: The frequency of a note, to use in the tone block. A4 is 440 Hz, C5 is one octave above C4.
ui.docs.more.ab_pitch:
Each sound inside this block gets a random pitch between the two numbers. 100 is the normal pitch, 90 is a little lower and 110 a little higher.

Sounds that are a little different every time are less boring to hear again and again, like jumps and footsteps.
ui.docs.more.ab_stop_sound: Stops all sound right away: effects, melodies and songs.
ui.docs.more.ab_play_song:
Plays a ready made song in the background while the game goes on. A song has four voices at once: melody, harmony, bass and drums.

Title theme, adventure, boss fight, menu, explore, cave, underwater, chase, shop, puzzle and castle are made to repeat. Level up, game over, victory, level start and secret are short tunes to play once. They end with a short rest, so they can also be played again and again. A new song replaces the one that plays. The song stops when the game is over or starts again.

Sound effects play on top of the song. On an Arduboy an effect borrows the harmony voice while it lasts.

An Arduboy plays all four voices, and so do other consoles with an ATmega32u4 and the speaker on pin 5 or 13. Other consoles play one voice at a time: the melody, or the harmony or bass when the melody rests. They leave out the drums.

The songs are played by ATMlib (Arduboy Tracker Music). The player takes about 3 KB of flash and 250 bytes of RAM, and each song 80 to 620 bytes of flash. They are only added when the game plays a song. On an ATtiny85, 250 bytes is half of the RAM.
ui.docs.more.ab_stop_song: Stops the song right away. Sound effects and melodies go on.
ui.docs.more.controls_if:
Runs the blocks inside only if the condition is true. With the version that has “else”, the blocks in the else part run when the condition is false.

Press the gear to add more “else if” parts. Conditions are the hexagonal blocks, like comparisons and “is button pressed”.
ui.docs.more.logic_compare: Compares two numbers and gives true or false. Choose in the list: equal (=), not equal (≠), less than (<), less than or equal (≤), greater than (>) or greater than or equal (≥).
ui.docs.more.logic_operation: Puts two conditions together. “and” is true only when both are true. “or” is true when at least one of them is true.
ui.docs.more.logic_negate: Turns true into false and false into true. “not mySprite exists” is true when the sprite is gone.
ui.docs.more.controls_repeat_ext: Runs the blocks inside a number of times. All the runs happen right away, in the same frame, so use it to build things, like placing ten coins, and not for things that should happen slowly.
ui.docs.more.controls_whileUntil:
Repeats the blocks inside as long as the condition is true, or until it becomes true.

The loop must end within the same frame, so do not use it to wait for a button. Use events for things that happen over time.
ui.docs.more.controls_for: Counts from one number to another and runs the blocks inside once for each number. The variable holds the number the loop has come to. Good for placing things in rows, like a row of bricks.
ui.docs.more.controls_flow_statements: Leaves a loop straight away (break out), or skips the rest of this round and goes on to the next (continue). Only works inside a loop.
ui.docs.more.math_number: A whole number. ArduCade uses whole numbers from -32768 to 32767, so there are no decimals: 7 divided by 2 gives 3.
ui.docs.more.math_arithmetic: Calculates with two numbers: plus, minus, times, divided by or to the power of. Division gives a whole number and the rest is thrown away.
ui.docs.more.ab_map: Converts a number from one range to another. For example, a value from 0 to 1024 becomes a number from 0 to 100. The result is a whole number.
ui.docs.more.ab_random: Picks a random whole number between the two numbers. Both numbers can come out. “pick random 1 to 6” works like a die.
ui.docs.more.math_modulo: The remainder after division. 10 divided by 3 is 3 with 1 left over, so the remainder is 1. Good for things that should happen every other or every third time.
ui.docs.more.ab_minmax: Gives the smaller (min) or the bigger (max) of two numbers. “max of life and 0” never gets below 0.
ui.docs.more.math_single: Does something with one number, for example removes the minus sign (absolute value) or turns plus into minus.
ui.docs.more.math_constrain: Keeps a number between a lowest and a highest value. If the number is too small you get the lowest, and if it is too big you get the highest.
ui.docs.more.variables_set: A variable is a box with a name that remembers a value, for example a sprite or a number. This block puts a value in the box. Make new variables in the Variables category.
ui.docs.more.math_change: Adds a number to a variable. Use 1 to count up and -1 to count down.
ui.docs.more.variables_get: The value that is in the variable right now. Use it wherever a number or a sprite is needed.
ui.docs.more.procedures_defnoreturn:
A function is your own block: a group of blocks with a name. Make it once and use it many places, so you do not need to build the same thing over and over again.

After you make a function, a block that runs it appears in the Functions category.
ui.docs.more.procedures_defreturn: Like a function, but it also gives back a value, for example a number it has calculated. The block that uses it is round and can be put where a number is needed.
ui.docs.more.ab_comment: A note for yourself or others who read the code. It does nothing in the game. Use it to explain what a part of the code does.
ui.docs.more.ab_comment_group: A note that holds a group of blocks, to show which blocks belong together. The blocks inside run as usual.
ui.docs.more.ab_cpp: C++ code that is copied straight into the game. For advanced users who know Arduino. It runs on the device, but not in the simulator.
ui.docs.homemade.title: Build your own Arduboy
ui.docs.homemade.body: Build a small game console with a Pro Micro and OLED. This guide follows ArduCade’s built-in “Pro Micro + SSD1306 (SPI)” profile. Follow the table and test one part at a time.
ui.docs.visual.arduboy.caption: An original Arduboy, front and back. Its screen has 128 × 64 pixels.
ui.docs.visual.first.title: Try a finished game first
ui.docs.visual.first.body:
1. Choose Platformer from the templates on the home screen or under New.

2. Press Play in the simulator. Move left/right and jump with A.

3. Open Blocks, Sprites, Tiles and Tile map. These are different parts of the same game. Change one thing, then press Play again to see the result.
ui.docs.visual.events.title: A small example: A adds one point
ui.docs.visual.events.body: Set score to 0 under “on start”. Put “change score by 1” under “on button A pressed”. Press Play and press A three times: the score becomes 3. Restart: it becomes 0. Each stack starts with the event that triggers it.
ui.docs.visual.code.title: A finished program, zoomed out
ui.docs.visual.code.body: This is the full block program from the Platformer template. Startup creates the hero and level; A events control jumping; other stacks handle coins, enemies and the goal. The respawn function groups the code for restarting after a hit. This view shows the structure; open the template in the editor and zoom in to read each block.
ui.docs.visual.sprite.title: 1. Draw and animate a sprite
ui.docs.visual.sprite.body:
Open Sprites and select hero in the Platformer template. It is 8 × 8 pixels. Draw with the pencil and use the colors or transparency to change pixels.

Select frame 1 and frame 2: the legs differ. Add frame creates another animation frame. The preview plays the frames in sequence. Use the animate block to play them in the game too. A drawing is an image; the sprite block creates an object with position, velocity and kind.
ui.docs.visual.sprite.caption: The sprite editor with the hero and two animation frames from Platformer.
ui.docs.visual.tile.title: 2. Draw ground tiles
ui.docs.visual.tile.body:
Open Tiles and select ground. Each tile is 8 × 8 pixels and can be reused throughout a level. Solid is enabled for the ground, so sprites collide with it.

The coin is not solid: the player must be able to touch it. A block event decides what happens on contact. Drawing a coin does not automatically award points.
ui.docs.visual.tile.caption: The ground tile is solid. Other tiles represent coins, spikes, the goal and enemy starting positions.
ui.docs.visual.map.title: 3. Assemble a tile map
ui.docs.visual.map.body:
Open Tile map and select level1. Choose ground in the palette and drag over the map to draw. Choose the eraser to make gaps. Pencil, line, fill and undo all have on-screen buttons for mouse and touch.

This level is 64 × 8 tiles, or 512 × 64 pixels. The screen shows only 16 × 8 tiles at once. The editor frame marks one screen; the game camera follows the hero through the rest. Column and row numbering starts at 0.
ui.docs.visual.map.caption: The Platformer tile map, with platforms, coins and gaps in the ground.
ui.docs.visual.connect.title: 4. Connect graphics to blocks
ui.docs.visual.connect.body:
Under on start, the template selects level1, creates a sprite using the hero image and Player kind, and places it at column 2, row 5. Move with buttons provides controls; camera follow scrolls the level.

When Player overlaps a coin tile, that tile becomes empty and score increases by 1. Add another coin to the map and play again. Each coin uses the same event.
ui.docs.visual.sim.caption: Platformer running in the actual simulator, with a screen and touch controls.
ui.docs.visual.test.title: Test one change at a time
ui.docs.visual.test.body:
1. Press Play and try left, right and A. On a tablet, hold right and A together to jump forward.

2. Find the A event in Platformer. Change jump velocity from −160 to −200. Press Play again: the hero jumps higher.

3. Touch an enemy, collect a coin and fall into a gap. Check lives, score and respawning. Use Restart for a new round. Keyboard controls are an alternative to the on-screen buttons.
ui.docs.visual.export.title: From simulator to handheld game
ui.docs.visual.export.body:
Select your device profile in Settings before compiling. Open Export and compile to get exact memory usage. A homemade device must use the pins in its profile.

Direct USB upload requires a browser with Web Serial and a supported bootloader. On iPad you can create, test and save the project; use a computer for USB upload. You can also download the Arduino sketch or HEX for transfer.
ui.docs.bom.title: Bill of materials (BOM) / shopping list
ui.docs.bom.tools: Reusable tools and programming equipment — buy only if needed
ui.docs.bom.pro.intro: For the USB-powered Pro Micro build shown in the schematic. Quantities are per console. Generic parts are specified by function and dimensions; no unverified manufacturer part number is assumed.
ui.docs.bom.tiny.intro: For one ATtiny85 console with two buttons and a four-pin I2C display. Quantities are per console. Tools and programmers can be shared between builds.
ui.docs.bom.pro.battery: Battery operation is not a completed purchasing specification yet: the two 3 V cell holders and three-pin switch are references until the wiring and regulator are verified. The reference 10 kΩ resistor is not needed for the shown circuit. No charger is included.
ui.docs.bom.tiny.resistors: No external button resistors are needed. No four-resistor display network is required for the specified complete OLED module. If the module has no I2C pull-ups, add two appropriate resistors (SDA to VCC and SCL to VCC); select their values for the module and bus before purchasing.
ui.docs.bom.pro-board.name: Arduino Pro Micro-compatible ATmega32U4 development board
ui.docs.bom.pro-board.spec: 5 V / 16 MHz; USB bootloader; micro-USB or USB-C. Not the 3.3 V / 8 MHz variant.
ui.docs.bom.pro-display.name: SSD1306 128 × 64 monochrome OLED SPI display module
ui.docs.bom.pro-display.spec: 7-pin, 4-wire SPI: GND, VCC, CLK/SCK/D0, DIN/MOSI/D1, CS, DC, RES/RST. Must accept 5 V supply and logic. A 4-pin I2C module does not fit.
ui.docs.bom.pro-buttons.name: 6 × 6 mm tactile momentary pushbutton, black actuator
ui.docs.bom.pro-buttons.spec: Normally open (NO), non-latching, four through-hole legs. Six buttons: Up, Down, Left, Right, A and B. Choose actuator height to suit the enclosure.
ui.docs.bom.reset.name: Two-pin momentary reset pushbutton
ui.docs.bom.reset.spec: Normally open (NO), non-latching, through-hole. Connect RST to GND; no additional pull-up resistor is normally needed on Pro Micro.
ui.docs.bom.piezo.name: Passive piezoelectric sounder / piezo buzzer
ui.docs.bom.piezo.spec: Two terminals, externally driven; rated for the console voltage (3 V ATtiny / 5 V Pro Micro). Not an active buzzer or low-impedance magnetic speaker. Optional if sound is not needed.
ui.docs.bom.usb.name: USB data cable for the Pro Micro connector
ui.docs.bom.usb.spec: micro-USB or USB-C to match the purchased board and computer. Must carry data, not charge-only. Also supplies power in this build.
ui.docs.bom.wire.name: Insulated hookup wire / jumper wires
ui.docs.bom.wire.spec: One assortment: male-to-male for breadboard; insulated solid-core hookup wire for soldered assembly. Lengths depend on the layout.
ui.docs.bom.board.name: Solderless breadboard or solderable perfboard
ui.docs.bom.board.spec: One board for the chosen assembly method; a breadboard is reusable for initial testing. Choose a perfboard large enough for the component layout.
ui.docs.bom.tiny-chip.name: Microchip ATtiny85-20PU microcontroller
ui.docs.bom.tiny-chip.spec: DIP-8 through-hole package; 8 KB flash / 512 B RAM; configured for internal 8 MHz, no bootloader. Check exact package when ordering.
ui.docs.bom.socket.name: 8-pin DIP IC socket
ui.docs.bom.socket.spec: DIP-8, 2.54 mm pin pitch, 7.62 mm row spacing; allows chip removal for programming or swapping games.
ui.docs.bom.tiny-display.name: SSD1306 128 × 64 monochrome OLED I2C display module
ui.docs.bom.tiny-display.spec: Four pins: GND, VCC, SCL, SDA; address 0x3C; must work at 3 V. SDA/SCL pull-ups must be fitted on the module or added externally. Not SH1106 or SPI.
ui.docs.bom.tiny-buttons.name: 6 × 6 mm tactile momentary pushbutton, black actuator
ui.docs.bom.tiny-buttons.spec: Normally open (NO), non-latching, four through-hole legs. Two buttons: Left and Right. Choose actuator height to suit the enclosure.
ui.docs.bom.cell.name: CR2032 3 V lithium coin cell
ui.docs.bom.cell.spec: One non-rechargeable cell. Do not replace it with two cells in series or a rechargeable LIR2032.
ui.docs.bom.holder.name: CR2032 coin-cell battery holder
ui.docs.bom.holder.spec: For one 20 mm diameter, 3.2 mm thick cell; two terminals; through-hole or wired, matching the mounting layout.
ui.docs.bom.switch.name: Miniature SPDT slide switch, three terminals
ui.docs.bom.switch.spec: ON–ON, non-momentary. Use centre and one outer terminal for on/off; leave the other outer terminal unused.
ui.docs.bom.capacitor.name: 100 nF (0.1 µF) ceramic decoupling capacitor
ui.docs.bom.capacitor.spec: Non-polarized, rated at least 10 V, through-hole. Connect directly between ATtiny85 VCC pin 8 and GND pin 4, close to the chip.
ui.docs.bom.programmer.name: ATtiny85-compatible AVR ISP programmer
ui.docs.bom.programmer.spec: Choose one: USBasp with target power suitable for the circuit, SparkFun Tiny AVR Programmer for DIP-8, or Arduino configured as ISP. Programming voltage must suit all connected parts; disconnect the coin cell.
ui.docs.bom.isp-wire.name: ISP connection cable / adapter
ui.docs.bom.isp-wire.spec: One set matching the programmer: RESET, MOSI, MISO, SCK, VCC and GND. A socket programmer may need no separate cable.
ui.docs.bom.solder.name: Electronics solder
ui.docs.bom.solder.spec: One spool; suitable for circuit assembly. Needed for the soldered build, not breadboard testing.
ui.docs.bom.iron.name: Temperature-controlled soldering iron
ui.docs.bom.iron.spec: One reusable tool for the soldered build.
ui.docs.bom.meter.name: Digital multimeter
ui.docs.bom.meter.spec: Continuity and DC voltage measurement, for polarity, switch contacts and short-circuit checks.
ui.docs.bom.cutters.name: Wire cutter / stripper
ui.docs.bom.cutters.spec: One reusable tool for preparing hookup wire.
ui.docs.bom.case.name: Enclosure or acrylic sheet for a custom case
ui.docs.bom.case.spec: Optional; dimensions depend on the finished layout. No fixed panel size has been validated.
ui.docs.bom.mounting.name: Enclosure mounting hardware set
ui.docs.bom.mounting.spec: Optional; M2 standoffs and matching M2 screws if compatible with the design. Quantity and lengths depend on the case.
ui.docs.visual.parts.title: 1. Gather the parts
ui.docs.visual.parts.body:
You need a Pro Micro with ATmega32U4, 5 V / 16 MHz and a USB bootloader; a 128 × 64 SSD1306 OLED module supporting 4-wire SPI (usually 7 connections); six pushbuttons; wires; a breadboard or perfboard; and a data-capable USB cable. A passive piezo is optional.

Choose an OLED module explicitly rated for 5 V power and signal inputs. A 3.3 V-only module needs the correct supply and signal level conversion. A 4-pin I2C screen does not match this guide’s SPI wiring.
ui.docs.visual.profile.title: 2. Choose the profile before wiring
ui.docs.visual.profile.body:
Select “Pro Micro + SSD1306 (SPI)” in ArduCade Settings. The table below reads directly from that profile. D means an Arduino digital pin; A0–A3 are the analog labels on the board. These are not physical microcontroller package pin numbers.

ArduCade uses OLED CS on D10 and a piezo between D5 and D9. MrBlinky’s standard Pro Micro wiring uses CS to GND and sound between D5 and GND; alternate wiring differs again. Use this table for this profile. For an existing build with different wiring, copy the profile and adjust its pins before compiling.
ui.docs.visual.wiring.caption: Vector components with color-coded wires and Pro Micro pin names. Battery holders, switch and resistor are unconnected references. Open the image for full size.
ui.docs.visual.power.title: 3. Connect ground and power
ui.docs.visual.power.body: Disconnect USB while wiring. Connect Pro Micro GND to the ground rail and OLED GND. For a 5 V-compatible OLED module, connect OLED VCC to Pro Micro VCC. Power this first version over USB; RAW is not VCC. Check polarity and that VCC and GND are not shorted before connecting USB.
ui.docs.visual.screen.title: 4. Connect the display
ui.docs.visual.screen.body: Connect CLK/D0 to D15, DIN/D1 to D16, CS to D10, DC to D4 and RES/RST to D6. Follow your module’s pin labels, not their order in a picture. SDA on some SPI modules means DIN/MOSI, not necessarily I2C. Do not connect CS to GND with this profile.
ui.docs.visual.buttons.title: 5. Connect the six buttons
ui.docs.visual.buttons.body:
Connect Up to A0, Right to A1, Left to A2, Down to A3, A to D7 and B to D8. Connect the other side of every button to GND. The program enables internal pull-ups: released is HIGH, pressed is LOW.

Four-legged pushbuttons often have pairs of legs already joined. Use a multimeter to find two legs that connect only while pressed. Test all six buttons, including two together.
ui.docs.visual.sound.title: 6. Add optional sound
ui.docs.visual.sound.body: Connect a passive piezo between D5 and D9. ArduCade generates the tone on D5 and holds D9 LOW. Do not connect a low-impedance speaker directly to the pins. The game works without a piezo, just without audible sound.
ui.docs.visual.upload.title: 7. Upload and test
ui.docs.visual.upload.body:
Connect USB with a data cable. Choose a small game or a guide with a movable sprite, verify the profile, open Export and press Compile. Upload from a computer with Web Serial. Follow the dialog to choose the bootloader port.

Test the display, each direction, A, B and sound separately before soldering. ArduCade uses its own game engine and generates ab_config.h from the profile; this upload does not require MrBlinky’s libraries.

Arduino IDE export uses the profile’s Leonardo target (ATmega32U4 / 16 MHz). Select the board’s port. An 8 MHz Pro Micro does not match the built-in 16 MHz profile. Keep the existing bootloader for your first build.
ui.docs.visual.trouble.title: If something does not work
ui.docs.visual.trouble.body:
Blank screen: check power, common GND, display driver, SPI mode and CS/DC/RST. Disconnect USB before changing wires.

Button always pressed: check which pushbutton legs are joined. Wrong direction: compare A0–A3 with the table. No USB port: try a data cable and follow the bootloader dialog.

Want a Nano with I2C? Select a Nano profile instead. Those use SDA=A4 and SCL=A5. ArduCade uses hardware I2C; do not directly copy MrBlinky’s I2C wiring to other pins.
ui.docs.visual.schematic.caption: Electrical schematic for the ArduCade Pro Micro profile: 7-pin SPI OLED, six buttons, passive piezo and reset. USB-powered; battery wiring remains unverified.
ui.docs.visual.supply.title: 3.3 V or 5 V?
ui.docs.visual.supply.body:
A console can use 3.3 V with a 3.3 V / 8 MHz Pro Micro and display and sound parts rated for that voltage. USB-C versus micro-USB does not identify the voltage variant. ArduCade’s current ATmega32U4 profile and browser compiler use 16 MHz; an 8 MHz board needs matching compilation, core and export settings. This guide therefore continues to use 5 V / 16 MHz.

Two 3 V coin cells give about 6 V in series or 3 V in parallel. Confirm the holder wiring, your board’s regulator and load before choosing a power connection. Never connect 6 V directly to VCC. A typical Pro Micro uses RAW as its regulator input, but voltage limits and dropout vary between boards. The battery holders and switch are shown unconnected here.
ui.docs.visual.reset.title: Reset button and resistor
ui.docs.visual.reset.body:
Connect the separate two-pin reset button between the board’s RST and GND. The OLED RES/RST still connects to D6 and is a different circuit. A Pro Micro normally has an onboard reset pull-up, so the external reset button does not need an additional 10 kΩ resistor. Game buttons use internal pull-ups.

The 10 kΩ resistor is a component reference, not a selected buzzer series resistor or power component. Appearance alone cannot identify an active buzzer, passive piezo or magnetic buzzer. The D5–D9 connection here applies to the passive piezo in this guide. Check specifications before connecting a different buzzer.
ui.docs.attiny.title: Build an ATtiny85 console
ui.docs.attiny.body: A tiny console with one 3 V coin cell, two buttons and an OLED display. This guide follows ArduCade’s ATtiny85 Pico profile. The component illustration and electrical schematic show the same circuit; physical pin numbers refer to the DIP-8 package viewed from above.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-parts.title: 1. Gather the parts
ui.docs.visual.tiny-parts.body:
You need a DIP-8 ATtiny85, an eight-pin socket, a four-pin I2C 128 × 64 SSD1306 OLED module rated to work at 3 V, two black 6 × 6 mm pushbuttons, a passive piezo, one CR2032 and holder, a mini SPDT power switch, a 100 nF ceramic capacitor, insulated wire and a breadboard or perfboard. You also need an ISP programmer or Arduino as ISP.

The reference build has two 1 kΩ button resistors. This ArduCade version does not use them: buttons connect to ground and the software enables internal pull-ups. A 100 nF capacitor is added for decoupling near the chip. An optional see-through case can use acrylic, M2 standoffs and screws.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-components.caption: Top-view ATtiny85, I2C display, buttons, piezo, battery holder and switch. Numbers after / are physical DIP pins. Open the image for full size.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-schematic.caption: Electrical schematic for ArduCade. Identical net names indicate the same connection even without a long wire joining the symbols. Buttons are active LOW.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-profile.title: 2. Select ATtiny85 Pico in ArduCade
ui.docs.visual.tiny-profile.body:
Hold the Settings button for five seconds with a mouse or finger. With a keyboard, focus it and hold Space. The extra settings appear; enable ATtiny85 Pico and save. This selects the profile for new projects. Also verify that the current project uses ATtiny85 Pico.

The profile uses the internal 8 MHz clock, 8 KB flash and 512 bytes of RAM. Left is PB0, right is PB2, and both together produce A. There are no separate Up, Down or B inputs. Start with a small game that fits these controls and compile to check exact memory usage.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-power.title: 3. Prototype the power circuit
ui.docs.visual.tiny-power.body:
Viewed from above with the pin-1 mark at the top left, pins 1–4 run down the left side and pins 5–8 up the right. VCC is pin 8; GND is pin 4. Use a socket and wire with the battery and programmer disconnected.

Connect battery positive to one outer SPDT switch terminal and the center terminal to VCC. Leave the other outer terminal unused. Connect battery negative to GND. Use a multimeter to identify switch contacts and verify the on/off action. Connect 100 nF between pins 8 and 4, close to the chip.

This circuit uses one CR2032, approximately 3 V. Two in series produce about 6 V and do not suit this circuit. ArduCade runs the ATtiny85 at 8 MHz; the datasheet requires at least 2.7 V for this speed range. Measure under display and game load because a coin cell may sag. Battery life has not been measured.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-screen.title: 4. Connect the display and piezo
ui.docs.visual.tiny-screen.body:
OLED VCC connects to switched VCC and OLED GND to common ground. SDA connects to PB3, physical pin 2. SCL connects to PB4, physical pin 3. ArduCade uses software I2C on these pins; do not copy the ATtiny’s usual USI/I2C pin assignments. The profile expects SSD1306 at address 0x3C.

Connect a passive piezo between PB1, physical pin 6, and GND. An active buzzer or low-impedance speaker may need a different driver and is not interchangeable with this piezo. Verify that both display and sound parts work at 3 V.

I2C needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL. This guide assumes they are already fitted on the OLED module. If they are absent, add one suitable pull-up from SDA to VCC and one from SCL to VCC. Four separate external resistors are not a general requirement; do not remove components already mounted on the display board.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-buttons.title: 5. Connect and test the buttons
ui.docs.visual.tiny-buttons.body:
Connect Left between PB0, physical pin 5, and GND. Connect Right between PB2, physical pin 7, and GND. The software enables internal pull-ups: released reads HIGH, pressed reads LOW. On four-leg pushbuttons, two legs on the same side are often connected; measure which contacts join only while pressed.

Test Left, Right and both together. Both produce A while Left and Right remain registered as pressed. Use the A event for firing, jumping or confirming a menu. Keep PB5, physical pin 1, as RESET for programming; it is not an extra game button.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-program.title: 6. Program the chip over ISP
ui.docs.visual.tiny-program.body:
This ATtiny85 build has no USB upload. Select ATtiny85 Pico, open Export, compile and download HEX. Transfer it from a computer using an ISP programmer.

With a socket, the simplest approach is to power off, remove the battery, carefully remove the chip and place it in a programmer supporting DIP-8 ATtiny85. Follow the programmer’s orientation mark. Many USB programmers supply 5 V; programming the chip alone avoids applying that voltage to a 3 V OLED or the battery.

For in-circuit programming, use RESET=pin 1, MOSI=PB0/pin 5, MISO=PB1/pin 6, SCK=PB2/pin 7, VCC=pin 8 and GND=pin 4. Game buttons and piezo share these pins. Remove the battery, do not press the buttons, and use supply and signal levels the entire circuit tolerates. Disconnect shared loads if necessary.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-clock.title: 7. Verify clock and fuse settings
ui.docs.visual.tiny-clock.body:
ArduCade’s HEX targets the internal 8 MHz oscillator with no bootloader. The game core removes CKDIV8 clock division at startup, so a factory-new ATtiny85 using its internal oscillator can be used. For a chip reused from another project, verify the clock selection.

ATTinyCore can set fuses: choose ATtiny25/45/85 without a bootloader, ATtiny85, internal 8 MHz and the correct ISP programmer. Keep RESET and ISP enabled. Burn Bootloader sets fuses even without a bootloader and may erase the program; transfer ArduCade’s HEX afterward. Choose a suitable brown-out level; 2.7 V is relevant for 8 MHz at around 3 V, but may cause resets when a CR2032 sags under load.

For USBasp, an example HEX upload command is “avrdude -c usbasp -p t85 -B 10 -U flash:w:spill.hex:i”. Replace the filename with yours. This writes flash, not fuses. Other programmers need their own correct names and settings.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-assemble.title: 8. Solder, enclose and swap games
ui.docs.visual.tiny-assemble.body:
After the breadboard version works, test-fit the parts on perfboard before soldering. Display, buttons, socket and piezo can face forward; battery holder and switch can be on the back. Check pin 1 and remember that the underside is mirrored when the board is flipped. Use insulated wire where it crosses other joints.

Test power, display, Left, Right, the A combination and sound before closing the case. Acrylic and standoffs can make a see-through enclosure showing the circuit. Keep the battery holder accessible.

To swap chips: power off, remove the battery and lift the chip evenly from its socket. Insert a chip programmed for the same circuit, internal 8 MHz and ArduCade button wiring. Games from other collections are not automatically compatible simply because they also use ATtiny85.
ui.docs.visual.tiny-reference.title: Differences from Instructables and the reference PDF
ui.docs.visual.tiny-reference.body:
The ATtiny85 Game Boy reference schematic, drawn by sunyecz06, uses one CR2032, piezo on PB1, SDA on PB3 and SCL on PB4. Those connections match ArduCade.

Its buttons connect to VCC with 1 kΩ pull-downs to GND. ArduCade expects active LOW and enables internal pull-ups. Connect buttons to GND and omit those resistors for ArduCade. This is an adapted circuit rather than a direct copy of the PDF. Programs from the original build may expect the opposite button logic.

ui.docs.more.ab_fx_pixel: Use single-pixel particles in this effect. Choose white, black, or a random black or white color for each particle. Put this part inside an effect recipe.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_image: Use a sprite image for particles in this effect and choose their color. Images with several frames play through their frames once over the particle lifetime. Put this part inside an effect recipe.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_life: Set the minimum and maximum lifetime in milliseconds inside an effect recipe. Each emitted particle gets a random lifetime in this range. 1000 milliseconds is one second; a lifetime of 0 creates no visible particle.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_direction: Set the direction in degrees inside an effect recipe: 0 is up, 90 right, 180 down and 270 left. Spread randomly varies the direction by up to this many degrees on either side. A spread of 180 sends particles in all directions.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_speed: Set the minimum and maximum starting speed in pixels per second inside an effect recipe. Each particle gets a random speed in this range. Use low values for smoke and high values for sparks.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_area: Set the width and height of the emission area in pixels inside an effect recipe. Particles start at random positions around the emission point. A size of 0 on an axis keeps that coordinate fixed; width 128 and height 0 makes a line suitable for rain.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_accel: Set acceleration inside an effect recipe: how much velocity changes each second, in pixels per second squared. Positive ax pushes right and positive ay pulls down; negative values push left or up. Use positive ay for gravity.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_drag: Set drag from 0 to 100 inside an effect recipe. Drag gradually reduces velocity in both directions: 0 adds no slowing, and higher values slow particles more strongly. Useful for smoke or explosions that spread and then slow down.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_wobble: Set wobble from 0 to 100 inside an effect recipe. Each frame adds a random change to horizontal velocity. 0 disables wobble; larger values make particles wander more, for example rising smoke.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_blink: Set the final percentage of particle lifetime during which it blinks, from 0 to 100, inside an effect recipe. 0 disables blinking; 30 blinks during the last 30% of its life. This makes particles flicker before disappearing.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_burst_from: Emit the chosen number of particles from the center of a sprite using an effect recipe. Rotation in degrees is added to the recipe direction. Existing particles move independently of the sprite. Use this in a button or overlap event for sparks; a destroyed sprite emits nothing.
ui.docs.more.ab_fx_clear: Remove all active particles made with the selected effect recipe. Other effects remain. The recipe is kept and can emit again; use clear all particles to remove every effect at once.
ui.docs.more.ab_shake: Shake the view for the given duration in milliseconds. Strength is the maximum offset in pixels, limited to 16; 1000 milliseconds is one second. This changes the view without moving sprites in the world. Use it for impacts or explosions.
ui.docs.more.ab_bg_set: Show a background image made in the Backgrounds tab behind the tile map and sprites. The image repeats to fill the screen and does not automatically follow the camera. Use the background position blocks to scroll it separately.
ui.docs.more.ab_bg_clear: Remove the background image. The tile map, sprites and other drawings remain. Choose a background again with the set background block.
ui.docs.more.ab_bg_set_position: Set the background offset in screen pixels. Positive x shifts the image right and positive y shifts it down; negative values shift left or up. The image repeats at the edges, independently of the camera. Set both to 0 to reset the offset.
ui.docs.more.ab_bg_change_position: Add pixel offsets to the current background position. Negative x scrolls left and positive y scrolls down. Use this in on game update for a continuously scrolling background, such as clouds moving behind the game.
ui.docs.more.ab_bg_x: Read the current horizontal background offset in pixels. This is the background offset, separate from the camera position. Use it in calculations to control background scrolling.
ui.docs.more.ab_bg_y: Read the current vertical background offset in pixels. Positive values shift the background down and negative values shift it up. This is independent of the camera position.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_set: Set one of the eight timers to a whole number of seconds from 0 to 32767 and reset its millisecond part to 0. The timer becomes visible. Setting a value does not start counting: use the timer run block to count up or down.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_change: Add whole seconds to the selected timer. A negative number subtracts time, without going below 0. The millisecond part is preserved unless a limit is reached. Use -5 to take away five seconds or 10 to award extra time.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_set_millis: Set only the millisecond part of the timer, from 0 to 999, keeping its whole seconds. This is not the total duration. For 2.125 seconds, set seconds to 2 first and then milliseconds to 125. The timer becomes visible.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_change_millis: Add milliseconds to the total timer value. 1000 adds one second and -100 subtracts a tenth of a second. Whole seconds adjust automatically when crossing a second boundary; the time stays between 0 and 32767 seconds.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_millis: Read the millisecond part of the selected timer, from 0 to 999. This is the fraction of its current second, not the total elapsed milliseconds. Use the timer value block to read whole seconds.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_run: Choose whether the timer counts up, counts down or stops at its current value. Counting down stops automatically at 0; it does not end the game. Check the timer value in on game update if reaching 0 should cause game over. The timer becomes visible.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_format: Choose how the timer is displayed: whole seconds, minutes or hours, mm:ss, hh:mm:ss, or either clock format with three millisecond digits. Hide removes only the display; counting continues. Whole minutes and hours discard the smaller units in the display.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer_position: Set the top-left corner of the selected timer display in screen pixels. x increases to the right and y downwards; the screen is 128 by 64 pixels. This moves only the display and keeps the timer value. It stays in place when the camera moves.
ui.docs.more.ab_info_position: Choose lives or one of the eight timers and place its display at x and y in screen pixels. The position is the top-left corner, independent of the camera. Moving the display does not change lives or time and does not make a hidden display visible.
ui.docs.more.ab_timer: Read the selected timer as a whole number of seconds; the millisecond part is omitted. Use it in comparisons, for example to end a round at 0. You can also plug this block into the sprite position block to move this timer’s display instead of a sprite.
ui.docs.more.ab_score_position: Set the top-left corner of the score display in screen pixels. x increases to the right and y downwards. The score stays fixed on the screen when the camera moves. This changes only its position; use a score set or change block to show the score.
