ui.docs.hardware.title: Supported hardware and custom profiles
ui.docs.hardware.body: This section describes the hardware targets available in ArduCade and how to match a profile to your device. A profile describes the microcontroller, display, buttons and sound. It does not change how you create the game.
ui.docs.hardware.support.title: What “supported” means
ui.docs.hardware.support.body:
Browser compilation means ArduCade can generate a HEX file using its bundled AVR compiler. Direct USB upload additionally needs a compatible bootloader and a browser with Web Serial; a USB connector alone does not guarantee upload support. Tablet users can configure profiles, run the simulator and export files; use a supported computer/browser or Arduino IDE for uploading when Web Serial is unavailable.

Arduino IDE export means ArduCade generates a sketch and configuration, but the target’s Arduino core and libraries must be installed separately. Export targets are not a promise that every board variant or module works. Check the actual variant, pin numbering and build report. Physical wiring, screen initialization, audio and upload behavior still need device testing.
ui.docs.hardware.memory.title: Clock, flash and RAM
ui.docs.hardware.memory.body:
Flash stores firmware and game assets. A bootloader uses part of the flash, and libraries also consume space. RAM holds working variables, sprites and graphics; the standard 128×64 one-bit framebuffer alone needs 1024 bytes. Leave RAM for the stack and runtime, rather than filling it to the limit.

The tables show values from ArduCade’s hardware definitions; KB here means 1024 bytes. On RP2040 and ESP boards, external flash capacity belongs to the defined board/module, not the microcontroller itself, and partitions reduce usable firmware space. Clock speed must match the board and Arduino build. The bundled ATmega cores are built at 16 MHz; ATmega32U4 at 8 MHz requires sketch export. Other architectures currently expose their defined clock only.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega32u4: The standard Arduboy target, with 32 KB flash and 2.5 KB RAM. Also used by Leonardo, Micro, Pro Micro and ItsyBitsy. Native USB uses a Caterina-compatible bootloader for supported uploads. The 16 MHz Pro Micro can use browser compilation; the 3.3 V / 8 MHz version requires Arduino IDE export. ItsyBitsy also requires export with the Adafruit variant. SPI uses D16/MOSI and D15/SCK; I2C uses D2/SDA and D3/SCL. Board pin availability differs, even with the same chip.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega328p: Used by Nano and Uno R3. Its 2 KB RAM is tighter than the ATmega32U4’s, so large levels and many sprites can exhaust memory. ArduCade can compile at 16 MHz and upload through a compatible serial bootloader. Nano bootloaders may use different baud rates. I2C uses A4/A5; SPI uses D11/D13. Nano A6/A7 are analog-only and cannot be game buttons or speaker outputs.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega328pb: A related AVR target with 32 KB flash and 2 KB RAM, but a distinct chip signature and Arduino core requirements. ArduCade has a browser compiler target and uses the first SPI/I2C units with the Nano-style pin map. Do not select ATmega328P just because a 328PB board resembles a Nano; verify the installed bootloader and pin numbering.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega644p: An AVR target with 64 KB flash and 4 KB RAM, useful for games that exceed smaller AVRs. Browser compilation uses the existing MightyCore/Sanguino-style mapping at 16 MHz. It is not Nano wiring: SPI uses D5/D7 and I2C D17/D16. Manual builds and uploads must match that core’s variant and bootloader.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega1284p: Provides 128 KB flash and 16 KB RAM. It uses the existing MightyCore mapping, including SPI D5/D7 and I2C D17/D16. The browser bundle lacks the required compiler libraries for this target, so export the sketch and build/upload in Arduino IDE.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega2560: The Mega 2560 target has 256 KB flash and 8 KB RAM. Its pin map is much larger: I2C D20/D21 and SPI D51/D52. It is export-only because the bundled browser compiler does not provide its architecture’s libraries. Choose the Mega target in Arduino IDE; Nano or Leonardo firmware is not interchangeable.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.atmega4809: The Nano Every target uses the megaAVR architecture, with 48 KB flash and 6 KB RAM in ArduCade’s definition. Its Arduino core differs from classic AVR and it is export-only. Similar-looking Nano boards are not necessarily ATmega328P devices; choose the correct board and core. The profile’s defined clock is 16 MHz.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.lgt8f328p: A Nano-like target with 29 KB flash and 2 KB RAM in the existing definition. It has its own core and hardware differences; it is not treated as a drop-in ATmega328P for browser compilation. Export and use the matching LGT8fx core and clock settings.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.rp2040: ArduCade’s RP2040 mapping targets Raspberry Pi Pico at 133 MHz, with the memory values shown in the table and a 2 MB external-flash definition. Export using the Pico Arduino core. GP labels mean GPIO numbers, not physical header positions. The runtime sets I2C GP4/GP5 and SPI MOSI GP19, SCK GP18, MISO GP16. Other RP2040 boards can have different numbering, flash sizes and exposed pins.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.esp32: The existing target is the classic ESP32 DevKit, not every ESP32-family device. It exports at the defined 240 MHz clock. SPI uses GPIO23/GPIO18 and I2C GPIO21/GPIO22. Pins used by flash are reserved; GPIO34–39 are input-only and need external pull-ups for buttons. Final memory use depends on the ESP32 core, libraries and flash partitions. ESP32-C3/S3 and other variants have no separate definitions here.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.esp8266: An export-only target at 80 MHz, with a dedicated ESPboy adapter as well as the generic OLED configuration. Generic I2C uses GPIO4/GPIO5 and SPI GPIO13/GPIO14. Several GPIOs are reserved for flash, and boot-strapping pins need correct startup levels. ESPboy uses an MCP23017 button expander and a ST7735 display; it cannot be configured as an AVR console. Install the ESP8266 core and Adafruit ST7735 and ST7789 Library for the ESPboy export.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.samd21: ArduCade uses the Arduino Zero mapping at 48 MHz, with 256 KB flash and 32 KB RAM. It is export-only. I2C uses D20/D21; SPI uses D23/D24. SAMD21 boards such as XIAO and Feather can expose different pins or variants, so the chip name alone does not establish compatibility. The definition has no EEPROM storage.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.stm32f103: The Blue Pill mapping exports at 72 MHz, with 64 KB flash and 20 KB RAM in ArduCade’s definition. Select the STM32 core and Blue Pill F103C8 variant. PA/PB names identify port pins rather than Arduino Nano numbers. I2C uses PB7/PB6 and SPI PA7/PA5. USB/debug pins are reserved in the editor, and the definition has no EEPROM storage.
ui.docs.hardware.chip.attiny85: A special, hidden Pico console target: 8 KB flash, 512 bytes RAM, 8 MHz, two buttons and software I2C on PB3/PB4. Its separate runtime draws the screen page by page. It can generate HEX in the browser but requires ISP programming, not the regular USB upload workflow. See the dedicated ATtiny85 guide when that setting is enabled.
ui.docs.hardware.boards.title: Development boards and presets
ui.docs.hardware.boards.body:
Development board mode chooses the microcontroller and clock together. Console presets include known display/button/audio wiring; bare development boards use example wiring or leave buttons unset. Match these defaults to your actual connections. Legacy profiles load in Microcontroller mode and keep their settings.

The table lists the board choices currently in the editor. The existing Nano + SH1106 preset remains available in the profile list. Arduboy FX, FX-C, Mini and Jr have no dedicated verified board definitions here: their external flash, display or optional hardware needs separate setup and testing. A familiar Arduboy name does not imply support for FX storage or every display variant.
ui.docs.hardware.displays.title: Screens and display drivers
ui.docs.hardware.displays.body:
Standard ArduCade games use a monochrome 128×64 display. Select the controller actually fitted to the module, not just its size or product name. Two OLEDs can look identical but require different drivers. A 128×32 panel, a color OLED or a generic TFT is not supported by the standard OLED runtime.

The bus must match the module’s wiring or solder-jumper configuration. I2C/SPI in the table describes the software driver; it does not mean every module exposes both buses. Rotation, mirroring and contrast change the image but cannot correct a wrong controller, resolution or wiring.
ui.docs.hardware.display.ssd1306: 128×64 monochrome OLED. The default driver used by Arduboy and many DIY profiles. I2C addresses are usually 0x3C or 0x3D.
ui.docs.hardware.display.sh1106: 128×64 visible monochrome OLED. The runtime handles its different display-memory layout and column offset. Use this driver when an SSD1306 setting gives shifted or corrupted pixels.
ui.docs.hardware.display.ssd1309: 128×64 monochrome OLED. Its initialization differs from SSD1306, including power/charge-pump handling. Check the actual module’s supported bus and voltage.
ui.docs.hardware.display.espboy: Dedicated ESP8266/ESPboy adapter for a 128×128 ST7735 TFT. Games stay monochrome 128×64, centered without scaling. It is not general ST7735 or ST7789 support. Original/Kit use an optional backlight DAC; DIY can use direct backlight wiring.
ui.docs.hardware.bus.title: I2C, SPI and pin names
ui.docs.hardware.bus.body:
I2C uses SDA and SCL plus power and common ground. Choose the displayed hardware bus pins and the module’s address. I2C is slower than SPI. Standard profiles do not offer arbitrary bus remapping; ESPboy’s separate adapter exposes its own bus fields.

SPI uses MOSI and SCK plus DC, optional CS and optional RST. DC selects commands versus pixels; CS selects the display, and RST resets it. Only leave CS unused when the actual wiring allows a permanently selected screen, and only omit RST when hardware reset is handled correctly. Fixed MOSI/SCK pins are shown in the profile form. MISO is not needed by the OLED itself but can still be claimed by the Arduino SPI runtime.

D/A names use the target’s Arduino numbering; GP/GPIO and PA/PB names use the specified architecture’s mapping. They are not physical package/header pin numbers. An analog alias can refer to the same physical pin as a digital name. Check the selected board’s pinout and module power/logic requirements; a profile does not convert voltage levels.
ui.docs.hardware.profile.title: Create your own profile
ui.docs.hardware.profile.body: Open a project and use Export → Change next to the device name. You can start from Custom profile, copy an existing preset, or load an .abprofile file. Configure the entire device in the same dialog; the steps below are a checklist, not a wizard.
ui.docs.hardware.step.open: Give the profile a descriptive name, for example “My Pro Micro OLED”. Built-in presets remain available; editing them creates your own copy.
ui.docs.hardware.step.target: Choose Development board for a listed board, or Microcontroller for custom hardware. In board mode the chip and clock are automatic. In manual mode choose the real chip and a supported clock. Check whether the summary indicates Arduino IDE export.
ui.docs.hardware.step.screen: Choose SSD1306, SH1106 or SSD1309 and the module’s bus. For I2C select its address. For SPI set CS/DC/RST and wire MOSI/SCK to the fixed pins shown. Set rotation, mirroring and contrast as needed. For ESPboy start from an ESPboy preset.
ui.docs.hardware.step.buttons: Assign Up, Down, Left, Right, A and B to your wiring. Standard buttons connect the input to GND when pressed and use pull-ups. Avoid reserved, bus and analog-only pins. Inputs without internal pull-ups need external pull-up resistors. ATtiny’s special runtime uses only Left and Right.
ui.docs.hardware.step.sound: Select Sound disabled for a silent device. Speaker selections are then hidden, saved for later and excluded from firmware. For sound, select the first speaker pin and an optional second pin matching your actual piezo wiring. A second pin needs a first pin. Do not drive a power speaker directly from GPIO.
ui.docs.hardware.step.validate: Read Checks and messages beside pin selectors. Resolve missing buttons, duplicated physical pins, reserved pins and bus conflicts before using the profile. Warnings about serial pins or external pull-ups also need checking against your wiring.
ui.docs.hardware.step.save: Press Use this profile to save it and apply it to the project. Save as file exports an .abprofile for backup or another device; Load profile file restores it. The project file also contains its hardware profile. Copy and edit keeps a reusable starting point; Delete profile removes a custom profile from your library.
ui.docs.hardware.step.compile: For supported AVR targets, compile and inspect flash/RAM use before uploading. For export targets, download the sketch, install the matching Arduino core/libraries and select the board and clock from the exported README. A mismatched F_CPU is rejected by the generated header. Test screen, buttons and sound on the physical device.
ui.docs.hardware.example.title: Example: Pro Micro 5 V / 16 MHz with SPI OLED
ui.docs.hardware.example.body: Select Development board → Arduino Pro Micro (5V / 16 MHz), then SSD1306 and SPI. The following wiring comes directly from the existing Pro Micro preset. Connect each game button between its listed pin and GND. Connect the piezo between the two sound pins only when using that two-pin sound setup. Share GND with the display and check the OLED module’s own supply/logic specification. These are example connections, not peripherals already installed on the Pro Micro.
ui.docs.hardware.manual.title: Example: a custom ATmega32U4 circuit
ui.docs.hardware.manual.body:
Choose Microcontroller → ATmega32U4 → 16 MHz. Select the display driver/bus and assign your own display control, button and speaker pins using the Arduino-compatible numbering in the profile. Keep hardware SPI D16/D15 or I2C D2/D3. No development board is inferred.

If the circuit runs at 8 MHz, choose 8 MHz and export the sketch. Use a matching Arduino core/variant and clock; the browser’s 16 MHz core cannot safely be reused by changing a single compiler flag. Raw chips also need an appropriate power, clock and programming circuit. A profile cannot install a bootloader or set clock fuses.
ui.docs.hardware.changes.title: Switching modes and restoring defaults
ui.docs.hardware.changes.body:
Switching from Development board to Microcontroller preserves the clock, wiring and other hardware settings. Switching back asks you to select a board explicitly; compatible custom wiring is retained. If applying a board, changing the chip/clock or restoring defaults would change hardware sections, the dialog lists them and asks for confirmation. Cancel keeps the configuration.

Restore board defaults reapplies known wiring. Rotation, mirroring and contrast are preserved. Check the displayed pins afterwards, especially when moving to a board with fewer exposed pins. Old profile files without board metadata stay in manual mode; ArduCade does not guess a board from the chip.
ui.docs.hardware.troubleshooting.title: When hardware does not behave as expected
ui.docs.hardware.troubleshooting.body:
Blank or shifted display: check controller, 128×64 resolution, bus, I2C address, reset and CS/DC wiring. Missing buttons: check the physical board pin map, common ground and pull-ups. No sound: check Sound enabled, speaker wiring and the profile’s selected pins.

Upload failure: check the bootloader, USB data cable, port permissions and browser support. Export-only targets need Arduino IDE. A game that works in the simulator still needs correct hardware wiring and enough memory on the device; use the actual compiler report and test on hardware.
ui.docs.debug.title: Debugging
ui.docs.debug.body: Debug tools let you pause the game, run one block or one frame at a time, and inspect what happens in the simulator.
ui.docs.debug.open.title: Open the debug panel
ui.docs.debug.open.body:
The panel stays hidden until you press the bug icon at the bottom right, above the memory summary and export section. This restarts the game and pauses before the first executable block.

The highlighted block will run next. Values show the state before that block. When paused at the end of a frame, no individual block is highlighted.

The bug button is hidden while debugging is active. Close with X at the top of the panel to show it again. The docked panel fills the area down to the export section.
ui.docs.debug.preview: Illustration of the detached debug window: the orange line is a drag handle. Execution controls and all four tabs use icons. The highlighted value changed since the previous pause. In the sidebar, the panel fills the width and has no orange line.
ui.docs.debug.controls.title: Buttons and icons
ui.docs.debug.inspect.title: What can you inspect?
ui.docs.debug.inspect.body:
Variables shows global variables and function parameters when paused inside a function. A highlighted value changed since the previous pause. Values are read-only.

Sprites shows active sprites with ID, kind, position x/y and velocity vx/vy. Positions are in pixels. Use this to investigate movement and collisions. The frame counter shows how far execution has progressed.

Messages shows runtime errors and notices about C++ blocks skipped by the simulator. Press a message to locate its block, if it still exists. The trash icon clears the list.
ui.docs.debug.breakpoints.title: Use breakpoints
ui.docs.debug.breakpoints.body:
Select an executable block in the Breakpoints list and press the circle-plus icon. You can also toggle a breakpoint from the block context menu. The block receives a red dashed outline.

Press Continue to run to that block. The game pauses before executing it, including repeated visits in a loop. Press a breakpoint entry to locate the block, or the adjacent cross to remove it. Breakpoints survive a restart but are not saved in the project or export.
ui.docs.debug.move.title: Move and resize the window
ui.docs.debug.move.body:
In the sidebar, the panel fills the section width without an orange line. Use Detach to open a floating window. You can then drag its orange left edge or Debug title with a mouse or touch. Dock returns it beside the simulator.

In the floating window, minus and plus change the height; you can also drag the resize handle. With a keyboard, Tab to the title or orange line and move with the arrow keys. Tabs use icons explained in the icon reference. All execution tools have on-screen buttons.
ui.docs.debug.limits.title: Execution and limitations
ui.docs.debug.limits.body:
Pause takes effect at the next block or frame end. A waiting block must finish before the next stop. Next frame runs until a frame completes, but a breakpoint may interrupt earlier. Closing the panel disables debugging and resumes paused execution. To end the game, press Stop first.

Debugging applies to the browser simulator. Raw C++ blocks do not run there, and physical hardware may behave or time things differently. The panel currently has no value editing, expression watches or call stack. Block navigation and breakpoints apply to blocks; text code has no line-by-line highlighting.
ui.docs.debug.example.title: Try it: follow a counter
ui.docs.debug.example.caption: Build these two events: set count to 0 at startup, and change count by 1 on each update.
ui.docs.debug.example.build: Create a variable named count. Put “set count to 0” in the startup event and “change count by 1” in the update event, as illustrated.
ui.docs.debug.example.open: Press the bug icon. Execution restarts and pauses before the first block. Open Variables and find count.
ui.docs.debug.example.step: Press Next block. The startup block runs, then execution pauses before the increment in the update event. count is now 0. Press again: the increment runs and count is 1 at the next stop.
ui.docs.debug.example.frame: Press Next frame to finish the frame in progress. Once paused at frame end, press Next frame again: the next update increases count once more. One frame step may execute several blocks.
ui.docs.debug.example.breakpoint: Add a breakpoint to “change count by 1”. Press Continue. The game stops before this block whenever the update event reaches it. Compare the value before and after a block step.
ui.docs.debug.example.inspect: Try this in a game with sprites: find a movement block, add a breakpoint and compare x/y and vx/vy in Sprites. If something fails, open Messages and press the error to locate its block.
ui.docs.debug.example.finish: Use Restart to repeat the experiment with the same breakpoints. Remove the breakpoint with the cross and press Stop when finished.
ui.docs.debug.action.show: Opens the tools, restarts the game and pauses before the first block.
ui.docs.debug.action.continue: Runs until the next breakpoint, pause or error. Starts the game if stopped.
ui.docs.debug.action.pause: Requests a pause at the next block or frame end.
ui.docs.debug.action.step: Executes the next block and pauses at the next block checkpoint. Also enters functions and loops.
ui.docs.debug.action.frame: Runs to frame end, or until a breakpoint is reached.
ui.docs.debug.action.restart: Restarts from the beginning and pauses before the first block. Keeps breakpoints.
ui.docs.debug.action.stop: Ends execution and clears the simulator display.
ui.docs.debug.action.toggleBreakpoint: Toggles a breakpoint on the selected block.
ui.docs.debug.action.detach: Detaches the panel so it can be moved freely.
ui.docs.debug.action.dock: Docks the panel beside the simulator again.
ui.docs.debug.action.disable: Closes the panel and disables debugging. Paused execution resumes.
ui.docs.debug.action.sprites: Shows active sprites, positions and velocities.
ui.docs.debug.action.log: Shows runtime errors and simulator messages.
